citation.author: Elpidorou, Andreas
citation.title: The Bored Mind is a Guiding Mind: Toward a Regulatory Theory of Boredom

discipline: philosophy of mind / affective science (analytic, empirically engaged; not Heideggerian)
thesis: Boredom should be understood as a functional, self-regulatory emotion that is both informative and regulatory of one's behavior: it informs the subject of the presence of an unsatisfactory situation and motivates the pursuit of a new goal when the current one ceases to be satisfactory, attractive, or meaningful. Adopting this regulatory perspective synthesizes the otherwise fragmented empirical literature on boredom's affective, cognitive, volitional, and physiological components, is consistent with evolutionary/functional accounts of emotion generally, and opens new, empirically testable predictions linking failures of the state-boredom function to the personality trait of boredom proneness.
sections: 1 Introduction (pp.455-457) -- motivates the topic via boredom's prevalence/cost; states the twofold informative/regulatory thesis

2 State boredom (pp.457-468) -- 2.1 Formal features (pp.458-460): duration, continuity, concreteness, susceptibility to situation, distinguishing state from trait boredom as a matter of kind; 2.2 The character of state boredom (pp.460-468): nine characteristics (a)-(i) from dissatisfaction through neural correlates; 2.3 Summary (p.468): compressed into four components -- affective, cognitive, volitional, physiological

3 Boredom as a self-regulatory emotion (pp.468-473) -- 3.1 Boredom as an emotion (pp.468-469); 3.2 The function of boredom (pp.469-471): twofold informative/escape-promoting function, self-effacing when successful; 3.3 The end of boredom (pp.471-473): self-determination theory, malfunction, and the normative limits of the regulatory 'call'

4 The value of a regulatory approach (pp.474-476) -- comprehensiveness/coherence; consistency with evolutionary accounts of emotion (three-part adaptive-value case); fruitfulness/testability (malfunction-to-trait predictions)

constructs.label: boredom-as-regulatory-signal (functional account)
constructs.treatment: the paper's entire argumentative object; developed across secs.3-4; every other construct is treated in service of this one

constructs.label: situational vs. trait/state boredom
constructs.treatment: four formal features (duration, continuity, concreteness, susceptibility to situation) individuate state from trait boredom as different psychological kinds, not degrees; standing critique that most research over-focuses on the (dependent) trait rather than the (prior) state

constructs.label: boredom proneness
constructs.treatment: trait construct operationalized by BPS (Farmer and Sundberg 1986) and ZBS (Zuckerman 1979), surveyed not administered; resurfaces as the paper's most concrete testable prediction via the locomotion correlation (Struk et al. 2016)

constructs.label: mind-wandering / task-unrelated thought
constructs.treatment: discussed under 'failure to sustain attention'; causal direction (precursor vs. consequence of boredom) flagged as an open question; possibly adaptive as a means of surfacing alternatives

constructs.label: attentional disengagement / meta-awareness
constructs.treatment: treated via Eastwood et al. (2012)'s 'unengaged mind' account under two of the nine characteristics (disengagement, attentional failure); later reinterpreted functionally rather than as mere deficit

constructs.label: flow / engagement (contrast pole)
constructs.treatment: Csikszentmihalyi's flow addressed directly and explicitly NOT treated as boredom's simple negation; Csikszentmihalyi's skills-exceed-challenge model of boredom is criticized as too narrow

constructs.label: monotony / meaninglessness
constructs.treatment: one of two ways a situation is 'non-optimal' (insufficient meaning or non-optimal challenge); recurs in the meaning-restoration discussion of sec.3.3

constructs.label: temporality of boredom (time-drag)
constructs.treatment: longest single-construct treatment in the paper; internal-clock (pacemaker/switch/accumulator) model; prospective vs. retrospective time estimation; arousal's complicating role

measures.label: self-report / survey scale
measures.treatment: BPS, ZBS, Fahlman et al. (2013) state-boredom scale, Goetz et al. (2014) five-point arousal Likert item -- all reviewed from the literature, none administered by this paper

measures.label: heart rate / HRV
measures.treatment: reviews Pattyn et al. 2008 (decreased HR during boring target-detection task), London et al. 1972 (increased HR and GSR), Chanel et al. 2008 (lower HR at easy/boring Tetris difficulty), Merrifield and Danckert 2014 (increased HR, decreased skin conductance) -- literature-cited only

measures.label: EEG alpha/theta power
measures.treatment: reviews Oswald 1962 (alpha waves during boredom), mental-fatigue alpha-increase literature, Tabatabaie et al. 2014 (lower left-DLPFC beta activity) -- literature-cited only

measures.label: EEG functional connectivity
measures.treatment: reviews Danckert and Merrifield 2016's fMRI comparison of rest, boredom induction, and sustained-attention task, all showing default-mode-network activation, with anterior-insular anticorrelation unique to boredom induction -- literature-cited only

measures.label: behavioral (RT / errors / performance-monitoring)
measures.treatment: reviews time-estimation paradigms (Watt 1991, London and Monello 1974) and Jiang et al. 2009's delayed frontal LPC/ERP responses in high sensation-seekers -- literature-cited only

readings.summary: No substantive engagement with FCM. Heidegger (1983/2001, i.e. The Fundamental Concepts of Metaphysics) is cited exactly three times, always bundled inside a string-citation with five or six other authors (Gabriel 1988, Greenson 1953, Hartocollis 1972, Tze et al. 2013, Wangh 1975, Watt 1991) in support of a single narrow observation: that boredom involves an altered, typically slowed, perception of the passage of time. There is no discussion of Dasein, Befindlichkeit, moods as ontological structure, the tripartite forms, or the two structural moments (Leergelassenheit/Hingehaltenheit). Given Elpidorou's demonstrated fluency with Heidegger elsewhere in this cluster (bor-sec-02 through bor-sec-06), this is read as a deliberate disciplinary choice to keep the regulatory-theory project inside analytic philosophy of mind/affective science, not an oversight.

concepts: self-effacing function (boredom dissolves itself when successful)
negativity bias / 'bad is stronger than good' (Baumeister et al. 2001)
self-determination theory: intrinsic vs. extrinsic motivation (Deci and Ryan 1985)
internal-clock model of time perception (pacemaker/switch/accumulator; Church 1984; Gibbon et al. 1984)
prospective vs. retrospective time estimation (Block and Zakay 1997)
default mode network (DMN) and anterior insular cortex in boredom vs. rest (Danckert and Merrifield 2016)
four formal features of psychological states vs. traits (duration, continuity, concreteness, situational susceptibility)
interlocutors: John Eastwood, Alexandra Frischen, Mark Fenske, Daniel Smilek (2012) -- 'The Unengaged Mind,' attentional-failure account of boredom's mechanism
Wijnand Van Tilburg and Eric Igou (2011, 2012, 2016, 2017b) -- meaning-regulation account; boredom's dissociation from anger/sadness/frustration
Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi (1975, 1990, 1993) -- flow / optimal experience, contrast pole and target of criticism
Edward Deci and Richard Ryan (1985) -- self-determination theory, intrinsic/extrinsic motivation
Roy Baumeister, Ellen Bratslavsky, Catrin Finkenauer, Kathleen Vohs (2001) -- negativity bias ('bad is stronger than good')
Barbara Fredrickson (1998, 2013) -- broaden-and-build hypothesis, positive emotions
Shane Bench and Heather Lench (2013) -- 'On the Function of Boredom,' cited and partly contested on the low-arousal/apathy reclassification move
Thomas Goetz et al. (2014) -- five-fold typology of boredom by arousal/valence, engaged with and ultimately not adopted
James Danckert and Colleen Merrifield (2016) -- fMRI default-mode-network study
Richard Farmer and Norman Sundberg (1986) -- Boredom Proneness Scale
Marvin Zuckerman (1979) -- Boredom Susceptibility Scale / Sensation Seeking Scale
Shelly Fahlman et al. (2013) -- state boredom scale; source of the 'gets us unstuck' formulation (p.68, quoted p.469)
Andrew Struk et al. (2016) -- locomotion/boredom-proneness correlation
Timothy Wilson et al. (2014); Havermans et al. (2015); Nederkoorn et al. (2016) -- self-administered electric-shock studies isolating boredom's escape-motivation
Martin Heidegger -- cited only in passing (three bare string-citations on time-drag); no substantive engagement
tensions: PRIMARY DEBATE-AXIS POSITION -- 'boredom-as-deficit <-> boredom-as-functional/adaptive' (this cluster's named axis; grounded here together with its companion piece bor-sec-26): Elpidorou does not caricature or dismiss a deficit reading of boredom -- he largely concedes its descriptive premises. Six of his nine characteristics of state boredom (dissatisfaction, disengagement, attentional failure, altered time-perception, ambiguous-to-negative arousal, felt constraint) are exactly the features a pure-deficit account would cite as evidence that boredom is nothing but psychological failure (pp.460-468). His argued move is not to deny these features but to reinterpret their functional significance: disengagement frees attention for something better; aversiveness gives the signal motivational force via the independently-established negativity bias (Baumeister et al. 2001, cited p.469-470); and the arousal ambiguity reflects two functional postures (low-arousal disengaging vs. high-arousal mobilizing) rather than a confound needing to be explained away (pp.464-466, 470-471). He lands squarely on the functional/adaptive side of the axis via a three-part adaptive-value case (self-regulatory flexibility is generally adaptive; narrowing the thought-action repertoire toward escape conserves scarce resources; boredom indirectly promotes the positive, resource-building emotion of interest) (p.474-475), while explicitly limiting the account's normative reach: boredom signals a lack of interest, not a lack of importance, so its regulatory 'call' must sometimes be resisted rather than obeyed (p.473).

Boredom's aversive phenomenology (conceded, extensively catalogued pp.460-464) vs. its functional payoff (argued pp.469-471) -- the tension is resolved not by denying the aversiveness but by showing, via negativity-bias research, why an aversive signal is precisely what a well-designed regulatory mechanism should feel like.

Low-arousal (apathetic, 'folk') reading of boredom vs. high-arousal reading vs. Elpidorou's own preferred 'both, depending on escape-availability' reading (pp.464-466): Elpidorou explicitly declines Bench and Lench's (2013) move of reclassifying low-arousal boredom as 'mere apathy,' and declines Goetz et al.'s (2014) five-fold arousal/valence typology, on methodological grounds (self-report-only arousal measures; unexamined temporal ordering; risk of conflating boredom with co-occurring emotions).

State boredom as conceptually and empirically prior to trait boredom vs. the field's actual research emphasis on trait boredom (p.457) -- Elpidorou treats this as a standing methodological criticism of the literature he is synthesizing, since trait measures presuppose an antecedent, less-studied state.

The regulatory function's success (escape into a more meaningful/interesting situation) is not equivalent to well-being (p.473): risk-taking activities can alleviate boredom while remaining costly or dangerous, so 'boredom was resolved' and 'the outcome was good for the subject' are explicitly treated as distinct evaluative questions.
